comments.author: @MorganTheGamerAndWriter
comments.text:
Spinning lady at ~16:45, the engine changes her dress from high neck to low neck, too. Cat at 32:32, there is not clear separation between the cat's trousers and the cat's foot shod or unshod foot.

I think the problems with AI video generation (similar to that of image generation) are that it is deviating from what has already been done. Once you start combining two different sources (like the giant sloth in the hoodie crushing buildings), it starts to get confused with what to do with all of that. I mean, sure, this is leaps and bounds ahead of what any of us envisioned computers being able to do in the 80s, 90s, or 00s... but, as it stands, humans are needed to create things in depth. For the time being.

Moreover, if this gets really good, and we can have more and more video content and games that are AI generated, it's just going to saturate the market. Who's going to watch it or play it? I think this will become less a replacement of human workers, but a dilution of human content consumers, as we are spread out between more and more content. Entertainment industries may become more and more challenged. Perhaps there would be some sort of resurgence of real experiences, kinda like the hipster movement but for entertainment. (shrug)

comments.text:
It is just a tool and it can be used to tell profound stories. We have played awesome games with awful graphic quality for decades.
However, many people seem to be just fooling around with those tools and are somewhat afraid to do anything serious, possibly because of the uncanny valley present in all AI-generated content and, of course, all the controversy around it. It's not clear if we even want it to ever reach the realism of real movies or not. It might be safer to use it for clearly generated art, animations, and stylized stuff, to at least avoid the uncanny valley. When watching an animation, we don't expect realism, so we digest small imperfections better.
